opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where people sometimes conflate a few different things.

At the most basic level, both autoregressive models and diffusion models are generative models: we train them to approximate a probability distribution over data. So in a sense, hallucination is just a symptom of the fact that the model's distribution isn't exactly the true one. The model puts some probability mass on things that look plausible, that are statistically consistent with the patterns it has seen, but that aren't actually grounded in facts. The model has no explicit notion of truth. It learns what text tends to look like. When it doesn't really "know" something, it still has to produce something, and the most likely-looking continuation might be a confident fabrication.

Then there are aspects specific to the architecture. With autoregressive models, you generate left to right, one token at a time, and you commit to every token. If you make a small mistake early on, maybe you sample a slightly wrong name or number, there's no mechanism to go back and fix it. The model then conditions on its own error and keeps building on it, trying to be consistent with what it already said. That's the classic exposure bias or error-compounding issue. It doesn't explain all hallucinations, but I think it contributes to the snowballing effect you sometimes see.

Diffusion models generate differently. You start from a noisy or masked sequence and refine the whole thing in parallel over multiple steps. That gives you, at least in principle, the ability to revise. The model can look at the entire output, notice that something is inconsistent, and correct it in a later denoising step. So you're not locked into early mistakes the same way. I'd say that's one of the more interesting potential advantages, for reasoning and for controllability, because you can steer the whole generation globally rather than only through the prefix.

But I want to be careful. Diffusion doesn't magically solve hallucinations, because the root cause, the gap between the learned distribution and reality, and the lack of grounding, is still there. If the model never learned a fact, no amount of refinement creates it. Diffusion models have their own failure modes too. When you generate many tokens in parallel, you're often making independence assumptions within a step, and that can produce incoherent combinations if you push too few steps.

So the way I think about it: part of hallucination is fundamental to learning a distribution from finite data, and you address it with better data, retrieval, grounding, calibration, teaching models to say "I don't know." Part of it comes from the generation procedure, and that's where I think diffusion gives us some genuinely new tools, being able to iterate, self-correct, and spend more compute refining an answer rather than committing token by token.

r001.rationale: It says hallucinations have a fundamental source in the gap between the learned distribution and reality, while generation procedure contributes separately, so architecture is not presented as the sole cause.

r002.rationale: It links hallucination to learning from finite data and lacking grounding, but does not identify extrapolation beyond training data as the condition that makes errors unavoidable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where people often lump a lot of different things together under the word "hallucination."

The way I think about it, the first and most fundamental source is just the training objective. These models are trained to maximize likelihood, to model the distribution of text they've seen. A model that's doing its job well is producing text that looks plausible given the data. But plausible and true are not the same thing. If you ask about a paper, the model has seen millions of citations, it knows what a citation looks like, and so it will happily generate something with the right shape, a realistic author list, a plausible venue, a title that sounds like something that person would write. From the model's point of view that's a perfectly good sample. It's not a failure of the generative process, it's actually the generative process working as intended. The problem is that nothing in maximum likelihood says "and by the way, only say things that correspond to facts in the world."

Then there's the second source, which is more specific to autoregressive models, and that's the way they commit to decisions one token at a time, left to right. Once you've sampled a token, you can't take it back. So if you make a slightly off choice early on, maybe you start a sentence in a way that implies you know a date or a number, you now have to fill in that date or number, and the model will do it even if the right behavior would have been to never start the sentence that way. There's this exposure bias, this compounding of errors, where you're conditioning on your own mistakes. And humans don't really write that way. We plan, we revise, we go back and fix things.

That's actually one of the things that got me interested in diffusion models for language. In a diffusion framework you're not committed to a single left-to-right ordering. You generate the whole sequence in parallel, you refine it over multiple steps, and you can in principle revisit a token you've already generated and change it. So structurally you have a mechanism for correction that just doesn't exist in the standard autoregressive setup. I want to be careful here though, because that doesn't magically solve the first problem. A diffusion language model is still trained to match the data distribution, so it will still produce plausible-sounding falsehoods. What it changes is the failure mode where you're trapped by an early mistake. And it opens the door to things like controllable generation, where you can constrain the output, or verify partial outputs during the denoising process, which is much harder to do when you're emitting one token at a time with no ability to backtrack.

There's a third piece too, which is the calibration question. Does the model know what it doesn't know? Pretraining tends to produce models that are actually reasonably calibrated in the sense of probabilities, but then post-training, RLHF and so on, often pushes them to be confident and fluent because that's what people rate highly. So you can take a model that had some internal signal of uncertainty and train that signal out of it. I think a lot of the hallucination problem, in practice, is a confidence problem rather than purely a knowledge problem.

So if I had to summarize: the root cause is the mismatch between modeling the distribution of text and modeling the truth. Autoregressive decoding makes it worse through irreversible commitment and error accumulation. Diffusion gives you a different sampling process that's more amenable to revision and control, which addresses that second part. And then whatever architecture you use, you still have to think hard about how to preserve or recover the model's sense of its own uncertainty, because otherwise you've built a system that's very good at sounding right.

r001.rationale: The response says hallucinations stem fundamentally from modeling text likelihood rather than truth, and that diffusion models can still produce falsehoods. This makes clear that hallucinations are not necessarily caused by architecture.

r002.rationale: The response discusses plausible but false output from the training objective, but does not identify extrapolation beyond training data as a source of errors or say such errors are unavoidable to some extent.

astra-6.text:
I think one way to understand it is to look at the objective these models are trained on. For an autoregressive language model, the objective is to predict the next token given the previous tokens. That’s not the same as checking whether a statement is true. You can produce something that is very plausible linguistically, that looks like the kinds of explanations you’ve seen in training, but that is factually incorrect.

Diffusion models have a different training objective—they learn to reverse a corruption process—but there’s a similar distinction. Learning a distribution over data doesn’t automatically give you a mechanism for verifying facts or enforcing constraints. A sample can look convincing while containing inconsistencies.

And there’s an ambiguity in what we call a hallucination. We want generative models to generate things they haven’t seen before. If you ask for an imaginary scene, that’s useful creativity. If you ask a factual question, inventing a plausible answer is a failure. So the challenge is getting the model to distinguish those situations, ground its answers in evidence, and recognize when it doesn’t have enough information to answer reliably.

r001.rationale: The response compares training objectives and says they do not verify facts, but it does not state that hallucinations are not necessarily caused by the choice of architecture.

r002.rationale: The response notes that models can generate things they have not seen, but it does not say that errors are to some extent unavoidable when a fitted statistical model extrapolates beyond its training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful starting point is that these models are trained to capture statistical regularities in data. They’re not explicitly trained to distinguish what is true from what is merely plausible. In an autoregressive language model, the objective is to predict the next token given the previous tokens. A statement can be very plausible under that objective and still be factually incorrect.

Diffusion models use a different process, learning to reverse a corruption process, but there’s a similar underlying issue: generating something that looks like the training data doesn’t guarantee that it satisfies every constraint we care about. An image can look realistic locally while having an inconsistent overall structure.

And I would distinguish errors in learning the distribution from the limitations of the objective itself. Even if you could learn the data distribution perfectly, that distribution contains mistakes, ambiguity, and conflicting information. So improving the model or changing the sampling procedure alone doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. You also need some way of connecting generation to evidence or checking the constraints that matter for the application.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared issue across diffusion and autoregressive models, but does not clearly state that hallucinations are not necessarily caused by the choice of architecture.

r002.rationale: The response says the data distribution can contain mistakes and ambiguity, but does not identify extrapolation beyond training data as a source of unavoidable errors.
